doc.title: Bernard Purdie interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

title: Friends versus associates; power over money
summary: He lost friends who turned out to be associates, says most conflicts were about power rather than money, and credits good teachers.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live

blocks.x: along because you think they’re friends. And when somebody is working with you or against you, they’re not a friend. Working with you is one thing. Working against you or working for themselves is a whole nother ballgame.
The times that those people that you thought were friends turned out not to be, was it usually a money issue? Power issue? Or can you pin it down?

Well for me, I’d say 95% of the time it was a power issue. It wasn’t even the money. Money makes power. But people who have money are really not interested or worried about making more money. They are interested in the power and what it does for them. And I got hurt a few times, I mean because of the power. I really truly did. But at the same time it was a major lesson for me that brought me through the business world. Because every time something happens — good, bad or indifferent — sshew, I could grab it and hold onto it. And it makes all the difference in the world when you can go back to it and relate to it, and just make yourself better, even if it hurts you, to stop somebody else from falling into that trap.

But I had good teachers. That makes the difference. It’s the teachers who give you the body, the instincts and things like that that you don’t have to be bitter, and you don’t have to be bad, because it happened to you. You can actually make it comfortable for somebody else. And in the long run it will make it better for you. It makes you a better person.
